en: Theragāthā 16.3 Vīsatinipāta Paṭhamavagga (The First Chapter)
The Verses of the Elder Telakāni:
“Truly, for a long time, being ardent,
I have reflected upon the Dhamma;”
I have not found equanimity for my mind;
I ask you, ascetics and brahmins:
"Who in this world has gone to the further shore?"
Who has reached the immersion in the Deathless?
To whom shall I teach the Dhamma that brings knowledge of the ultimate truth?”
He entered into a crooked place like a fish seeking bait;
he was caught by the great Indra’s snare.
Like the asura Vepacitti,
I pull him toward me and do not let him go,
from this lamentation and wailing.
Who in this world will release me from bondage and make me realize full enlightenment?
Which ascetic or brahmin [will do so]?
To whom shall I listen to the Dhamma— teaching that which is beginningless, subject to destruction,
and the driver away of old age and death?
Bound by the fetters of doubt and uncertainty,
constrained by the force of aggression,
with a mind hardened by anger and resentment—
The shattering of longing,
arising from the bow of craving,
and the two [sections] consisting of fifteen [verses] each.
Behold how it remains firm, having broken through the chest;
such is the non-abandoning of dogmatic views.
Whetted by the power of intention; pierced by it,
I tremble like a leaf stirred by the wind.
Arising within myself,
it quickly ripens for me;
the body consists of the six bases of contact.
I do not see any remedy for that which always brings one back to memory,
were it not for him who could pull out this arrow from me.
Not by a sword with many edges, nor by any other weapon, can doubt be pierced.
Who is my surgeon? Who is my healer?
The arrow lodged within my side,
the non-harming one who will extract the arrow from all my limbs.
For he is the supreme physician,
who carries away the poison of defilements;
for me, who had fallen into the deep, [he is the savior].
He showed me dry land and his hand.
I had plunged into a lake of dust and soil that was not to be taken away.
Deceit, envy, and aggression,
enveloped by sloth and torpor;
agitation is like the thundering of clouds.
A cloud of fetters;
the currents carry away one of evil views,
whose intentions are based on passion.
Everywhere streams flow;
a creeper grows up and stands firm.
Who could stop those streams?
For who indeed could cut that creeper?
O venerable ones, make a dam to block the flow of the streams.
Let not your mind-made stream be suddenly lopped off like a tree;
thus [I speak] to me who am filled with fear.
The Teacher, who has gone from this shore to the further shore, is the refuge, armed with the weapon of wisdom,
and served by the assembly of seers.
You have provided a well-constructed, pure,
and firm staircase made of the essence of Dhamma for one who is being swept away.
"Do not fear," he said to me.
Having ascended the palace of the foundations of mindfulness, I reflected.
That which I previously thought was the people’s delight in self-identity—
when I beheld the path, [I saw it as such].
Having embarked upon the boat,
and without clinging to a self,
I beheld the supreme landing place.
The arrow arising from oneself,
produced by the conduit of existence—
for the non-occurrence of these, [one should practice].
He taught the supreme path—
that which has been latent for a long time and firmly established for a long time.
“May the Buddha dispel my bondage,
he who carries away the poison of defilements.
… Thus spoke the Elder Telakāni.
